title: Baku and not baku — the Indonesian of the dictionary
goal: Tell standard (*baku*) Indonesian from the everyday forms around it, use KBBI and EYD as your referees, and stop making the handful of spelling and word-form errors that even educated Indonesians make in writing.
bekal: fix the classic errors on sight: *merubah → mengubah*, *praktek → praktik*, *antri → antre*, *ijin → izin*
switch between Fajar's Jakarta Indonesian and the register of an official document without mixing the two
tell the prefix *di-* (*dikirim*) from the preposition *di* (*di kementerian*) and write each one correctly

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hari pertama di Program Jembatan
dialogs.intro: Monday, 8 January 2029. Sarah is back in Jakarta, this time as director of Program Jembatan, an Australia–Indonesia education exchange with an office in Kuningan. Her deputy Fajar, born and bred in Condet, shows her to her desk.

notes: **Balik, udah, aja, nggak, gimana — Jakarta on a Monday morning.** Fajar and Sarah talk the way Jakarta offices talk between colleagues. The standard equivalents are *kembali, sudah, saja, tidak, bagaimana*. None of the spoken forms would survive in the profile they are about to correct, and that contrast is the subject of this whole unit.

**Siapin, nulis, ngecek, nyoret — the spoken verb.** Jakarta speech drops the *me-* prefix, keeps only its nasal sound, and swaps *-kan* for *-in*: *siapin* = *menyiapkan*, *nulis* = *menulis*, *ngecek* = *mengecek*, *nyoret* = *mencoret*. Understand them instantly; write only the standard ones.

**Nggak enak** is the B1 feeling of social awkwardness, not “not tasty”. Fajar cannot bring himself to call his director by her bare first name. Sarah's compromise, *Bu* in meetings and first names in the pantry, is exactly how many Jakarta offices settle it. Within a few weeks Fajar will drift to the halfway house, *Mbak*, which is what Yoga already calls her.

**Beliau** is the respectful “he/she”. Fajar uses it for Ibu Maria even in a chatty sentence, and switches to careful standard words (*Bukan galak. Teliti.*) the moment he talks about her. Respect pulls the register up, even mid-conversation.

**KBBI daring.** The *Kamus Besar Bahasa Indonesia* is the official dictionary, published by the Badan Bahasa (the national language agency). *Daring* is short for *dalam jaringan*, “in the network”, the official word for “online”; its opposite is *luring*, *luar jaringan*, “offline”. When two Indonesians argue about a word, KBBI settles it.

**Siap! and Deal.** *Siap* (“ready!”) comes from the army and is now the office's eager “yes, boss”. *Deal* is plain English, and educated Jakartans sprinkle English like this through casual speech. Both are fine in the pantry and both are out of place in a letter.

grammars.title: The classic errors
body: *Baku* means standard: the form KBBI lists as its main entry and that the spelling rules (EYD) support. Non-baku forms are everywhere on signs, in chats and even in newspapers, but in a letter, a report or an exam they count as mistakes.
after: ⚠️ *Merubah* is the most famous mistake in the language. The root is *ubah*, and *me- + ubah* gives *mengubah*, just as *ambil* gives *mengambil*. The *r* in *berubah* (to change, intransitive) and *perubahan* (a change) belongs to the prefixes *ber-* and *per-*, not to the root.

Once the root is right, the whole family follows: *antre → antrean, mengantre*; *izin → mengizinkan, perizinan*; *praktik → praktikum*. Look up a doubtful word in KBBI daring and a non-baku spelling will send you to the baku one.

grammars.title: The same sentence in two registers
body: Baku is the default for anything written or official. Below are Fajar's sentences as he said them, and as they would appear in a document.

head: Fajar says
Written standard
English
rows: Ibu Maria will cross it out at once.

after: Notice how little changes: a handful of small words (*udah/sudah, aja/saja, gimana/bagaimana*) and the verb prefix. The grammar underneath is the same, which is why Indonesians can switch register in the middle of a sentence.
⚠️ What gives a learner away is the half-and-half sentence: *Saya belum mengecek, soalnya laptopnya error banget* is neither register. Choose one per text, and in anything written, choose baku.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Coretan merah Ibu Maria
dialogs.intro: Thursday, 11 January. The profile went to the ministry on Tuesday. Today Ibu Maria Simanjuntak, head of the international cooperation section, has asked Sarah to her office in Senayan. The draft on her desk is covered in red ink.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Silakan duduk, Ibu Sarah. Saya langsung saja, ya. Draf ini belum bisa kami terima.
lines.id: Please sit down. I'll come straight to the point. We can't accept this draft yet.
lines.literal: please sit, Mrs Sarah. I direct just, [ya]. draft this not-yet can we accept.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Baik, Bu. Bagian mana yang perlu diperbaiki?
lines.id: Of course. Which parts need correcting?
lines.literal: good, Mrs. part which that need be-corrected?

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Hampir semua halaman. Di sini tertulis ‘merubah kurikulum’. Yang benar ‘mengubah’.
lines.id: Almost every page. Here it says ‘merubah kurikulum’. The correct form is ‘mengubah’.
lines.literal: almost all page. at here is-written ‘merubah curriculum’. that correct ‘mengubah’.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Mohon maaf, Bu. Itu kesalahan kami.
lines.id: My apologies. That's our mistake.
lines.literal: beg pardon, Mrs. that mistake our.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Lalu ‘praktek mengajar’, ‘surat ijin’, ‘nomor antri’. Semuanya tidak baku.
lines.id: Then ‘praktek mengajar’, ‘surat ijin’, ‘nomor antri’. None of it is standard.
lines.literal: then ‘practice teach’, ‘letter permit’, ‘number queue’. all-of-it not standard.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kami akan menyesuaikannya dengan KBBI dan EYD, Bu.
lines.id: We'll bring it into line with KBBI and EYD.
lines.literal: we will adjust-it with KBBI and EYD, Mrs.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Bagus. Satu lagi: ‘di kirim’ ditulis terpisah. Awalan ‘di-’ harus ditulis serangkai.
lines.id: Good. One more thing: ‘di kirim’ is written as two words. The prefix ‘di-’ must be joined on.
lines.literal: good. one more: ‘di kirim’ is-written separate. prefix ‘di-’ must is-written joined.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dan ‘di kementerian’ tetap dipisah karena itu kata depan, betul, Bu?
lines.id: And ‘di kementerian’ stays separate because it's a preposition, right?
lines.literal: and ‘at ministry’ stay is-separated because that word front, correct, Mrs?

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Betul sekali. Ternyata Ibu lebih teliti daripada draf Ibu.
lines.id: Exactly. It turns out you're more careful than your draft.
lines.literal: correct very. turns-out Mrs more meticulous than draft Mrs.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Bu. Versi perbaikannya kami kirimkan hari Senin.
lines.id: Thank you. We'll send the corrected version on Monday.
lines.literal: thank-you, Mrs. version correction-its we send Monday.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Saya tunggu. Tulisan yang rapi itu tanda hormat, Ibu Sarah.
lines.id: I'll be waiting. Tidy writing is a sign of respect, Sarah.
lines.literal: I wait. writing that tidy that sign respect, Mrs Sarah.

notes: **Saya langsung saja.** Ibu Maria is Batak, and Batak directness is a well-known Indonesian stereotype that she happily lives up to. Notice, though, that her directness stays entirely inside baku Indonesian: *Ibu Sarah* for “you”, *kami* for the ministry, not a single slang word.

**Belum bisa kami terima** — “cannot yet be accepted by us”. This is the object-first passive from A1 with *kami* before a bare verb. *Belum* is the diplomatic word here: not “no”, but “not yet”, which leaves the door open.

**Kesalahan kami, kami kirimkan.** Both women speak for their institutions, so both use *kami* (we, not including you). In formal Indonesian the institution is always *kami*; *saya* is only the person. Sarah apologises on behalf of the programme, not personally.

**Tertulis** — “it is written, it says”. *Ter-* here describes a state, not an accident. *Yang benar* (“the correct one”) is how teachers and editors introduce a correction; *yang salah* is the wrong one.

**Menyesuaikannya dengan** — “to adjust it to, bring it into line with”, from *sesuai* (appropriate, in accordance). This is the go-to verb for fixing a document to a standard: *disesuaikan dengan aturan*, *sesuai dengan KBBI*.

**Lebih teliti daripada draf Ibu.** Ibu Maria's one joke, delivered deadpan. *Daripada* is the correct word for “than” in comparisons, and it is written as one word; Unit 2 deals with the ways it gets misused.

grammars.title: Di-: prefix or preposition?
body: The test is simple. If the word after *di* is a place and you could ask *di mana?* about it, *di* is a preposition and stands apart. If the word after it is a verb, *di-* is the passive prefix and is joined on.
after: *Ke* follows the same logic: *ke kantor* (to the office) is two words, *kedua* (second) and *kesalahan* (mistake) are one. ⚠️ *Keluar* (to exit) is one word; *ke luar negeri* (abroad) is three.
The particle *pun* has a rule of its own: it is joined in fixed conjunctions (*walaupun, meskipun, bagaimanapun*) and separate after ordinary words (*apa pun, siapa pun, satu huruf pun*).

blocks.text: These are the words Indonesian editors correct most often. The left-hand forms are what you will see on shop signs and in chats; the right-hand forms are what KBBI lists and what an exam expects.

items: More for your list: *aktifitas → aktivitas*, *obyek → objek*, *frekwensi → frekuensi*, *telpon → telepon*, *himbau → imbau*, *cabe → cabai*, *standarisasi → standardisasi*.
⚠️ *Silahkan* with an *h* is so common on signs that many Indonesians are surprised to learn it is wrong. The root is *sila*, “please, be so kind”, so the word is *silakan*, with no *h* anywhere.

sections.title: KBBI, EYD and the Badan Bahasa

blocks.text: Standard Indonesian has official referees, and Indonesians take them seriously. Sarah will meet all of them again when she sits the UKBI, the national proficiency test, at the end of this book.

blocks.text: Baku is not the same as “correct” in every situation. Saying *Saya tidak mengetahui* to a friend over coffee is perfectly baku and slightly absurd. The skill this book trains is choosing: baku where the situation asks for it, everyday speech where it does not.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
